name: Ridgelet Transform Analysis
description: Applies ridgelet transform for detecting line singularities and edge structures in AI-generated images (Candès & Donoho, 1999).
mechanism:
This method applies the ridgelet transform — optimal for representing line singularities — to extract directional edge features for distinguishing natural from AI-generated images:

1. **Radon Transform**: The ridgelet transform is computed by first applying the Radon transform R to the image: Rf(θ, t) = ∫∫ f(x,y) δ(x cos θ + y sin θ − t) dx dy. This projects the image intensity along lines at angle θ and offset t, converting line features in 2D into point features in Radon space. For images with block structure, the finite Radon transform (FRAT) is used on B×B subblocks (typically B = 16 or 32).

2. **1D Wavelet on Radon Projections**: For each angle θ, a 1D wavelet transform is applied to the Radon projection Rf(θ, ·) along the offset variable t: Ridgelet(a, b, θ) = a^(−1/2) ∫ Rf(θ, t) ψ((t − b)/a) dt, where ψ is the mother wavelet (typically a Mexican hat or Meyer wavelet), a is the scale parameter, and b is the translation. The ridgelet coefficients capture line singularities at specific orientations, scales, and positions.

3. **Coefficient Distribution Analysis**: The distribution of ridgelet coefficients is analyzed for forensic features. Natural images have ridgelet coefficient distributions that are well-modeled by generalized Gaussian distributions (GGD) with shape parameter β ∈ [0.3, 0.8] — heavy-tailed distributions reflecting the sparsity of line features. AI-generated images often show: (a) higher β values (more Gaussian-like) due to smoother edge statistics, (b) different scale-dependent decay rates, and (c) anomalous orientation selectivity patterns reflecting GAN/diffusion architecture biases.

4. **Directional Feature Extraction**: The ridgelet energy is computed per orientation bin: E(θ) = Σ_{a,b} |Ridgelet(a,b,θ)|². The orientation energy histogram reveals directional preferences in the image structure. Natural photographs show content-dependent orientation distributions, while AI-generated images often exhibit subtle biases toward horizontal and vertical orientations (0°, 90°) inherited from the convolutional architecture. The Kullback-Leibler divergence between the observed orientation histogram and a reference natural image model quantifies the anomaly.
parameters:
Block size: 16×16 or 32×32 pixels
Radon transform: finite (FRAT) on subblocks
Wavelet: Mexican hat, 5 scales
Orientation bins: 18 (10° resolution)
GGD shape parameter threshold: β = 0.9
KL divergence threshold: D_KL > 0.15
Minimum image size: 128×128 pixels
accuracy: 77–85% accuracy for AI-generated image detection using ridgelet features alone. GGD shape parameter classification achieves AUC of 0.84. Directional energy analysis adds 3–5% improvement when combined with coefficient statistics. Performance is best on images with prominent edge structures and weakest on highly textured content.
source: Candès, E. J. & Donoho, D. L. (1999). Ridgelets: A Key to Higher-Dimensional Intermittency? Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A, 357(1760), 2495–2509.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images through directional edge structure analysis. Analyzing line singularity patterns in architectural and urban photographs. Feature extraction for machine learning forensic classifiers. Multi-resolution directional analysis complementary to wavelet-based methods.
strengths:
• Ridgelets are optimal for representing line singularities — superior to wavelets for edges
• Orientation-selective analysis captures directional biases of AI generators
• GGD shape parameter provides a compact, scale-invariant feature
• Complements wavelet-based methods by capturing features wavelets miss
• Well-established mathematical framework from harmonic analysis
limitations:
• Block-based ridgelet transform introduces blocking artifacts at subblock boundaries
• Performance is weaker on images without prominent edge structures
• Higher computational cost than standard wavelet transforms
• AI generators with advanced architecture (attention mechanisms) reduce directional biases
• Requires careful scale/orientation parameter tuning for different image types
